newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral worried about ailing infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral worried about ailing infrastructure.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral expressed concern on Monday over bottlenecks in the creaking infrastructure sector which he believes are hampering economic expansion.

"The Prime Minister was concerned that there was a shortfall in crucial infrastrucure sectors," Planning Commission deputy chairman Madhu Dandavate quoted Gujral as saying at his first meeting with top planners.
Officials said Gujral, who is also the chairman of the Planning Commission, asked authorities to step up implementation of power projects across the country.
"Unless we are able to pick up this one dimension of energy, we are nowhere," a statement quoted Gujral as saying.

The independent Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) said in its review of the economy on Monday that power generation grew by only 3.1 percent to 33,063 megawatts (MW) in 1996/97 (April-March) from 32,074 MW in the previous year.
The government plans to tap hydroelectric power, wherever available, to boost capacity, Dandavate said.
He said in India's Ninth Plan for 1997-2002 about 40,000 MW of additional power is expected to be generated compared with an official estimate of 57,000 MW.
In the Eighth Plan for 1992-97, only 17,000 MW was added to the national grid against a target of 30,000 MW.
"The states must reform their electricity boards and rationalise tariffs," Dandavate said.
Many states were giving free power to farmers, leading to massive subsidies and affecting the performance of state electricity boards, he said. "This must stop."
Dandavate said federal assistance may not be made available to states which fail to rationalise tariffs and do not reform their state electricity boards.
Industry leaders have said slow growth in the infrastructure sector, particularly power, would hit industrial growth.
Industry is expected to show about four percent growth in the 1996/97 fiscal year, the CMIE said in its monthly review for May.
The CMIE had in January forecast industrial output to grow at six percent in 1996/97, down from its previous estimate of seven percent.
India's government expects industry to grow at 8.7 percent in 1996/97 compared with 11.6 percent in the previous year.

"CMIE's expectation of 6.0-7.0 percent industrial output was based on the premise that industrial activity would pick up in response to lower interest rates and a better agricultural crop," the CMIE report said.
It said that while interest rates declined and the agriculture crop turned out to be good, industrial output did not grow as predicted.
"The delay in the industrial revival implies a longer inventory cycle than anticipated earlier," the CMIE said. The expected second half recovery was much lower than anticipated, it added.
